title: Human dignity (CCC 1700, 1929–1933)
hookLine: every person's dignity comes from God, not from usefulness

cards: Rome, in a time of persecution. A Roman official hears that the Church has treasure. He summons Lawrence, the deacon who looks after the Church's money, and demands it.
Lawrence promises to show him. The story, as Ambrose tells it, is that the next day Lawrence came back with a crowd: the poor the Church fed. Asked where the treasure was, he pointed at them.
These, he said, are the treasures of the Church. The official was not amused, and Lawrence was martyred. Catholics still tell the story on his feast day.

teach.b: The Catechism opens its whole teaching on the moral life here: the dignity of the human person is rooted in being created in the image and likeness of God. Remember imago Dei, earlier on the path? This is where it leads.
Dignity isn't earned, voted on or measured. It's given, by God, to everyone.
If dignity came from usefulness, the productive, the healthy, the clever and the rich would be worth more.

The letter of James pictures a man with a gold ring getting a good seat in the assembly while a poor man in shabby clothes is told to stand over there, or sit on the floor, and calls it judging with unjust thoughts.
Worth, the Church says, doesn't come from what you can do. The newborn, the person with dementia, the unborn, the prisoner, the migrant, the dying: none of them has less.
The Catechism asks everyone to look on the neighbor, without exception, as another self, and to take their life, and what they need to live it with dignity, into account.
Social justice, it says, can only be built by respecting that dignity. And the respect reaches those who think or act differently from us.
The Catechism quotes Jesus in the Sermon on the Mount: "Love your enemies: do good to them that hate you."

teach.h: THESE ARE THE TREASURES OF THE CHURCH.
teach.b: Dignity doesn't switch off when someone becomes hard to like. Lawrence knew the Church's treasure wasn't in a vault. It was walking around, hungry, in the streets of Rome.

how: Human dignity is the foundation of Catholic social teaching; parishes and Catholic charities apply it in care for the poor, the sick, the unborn, the elderly, migrants and prisoners, and Catholics keep a feast of St. Lawrence each August.

o: a calm, proud way of carrying yourself
the respect a person earns by good conduct
the worth every person has, given by God

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: brought the poor as the Church's treasure
the gold ring and the shabby clothes
dignity even for those against us

s: in Catholic teaching, dignity grows with what a person can do
the Catechism roots dignity in God's image, given to everyone, not in usefulness.
the Catechism says respect reaches even those who think differently
it extends to those who think or act differently, and to enemies.
the story of Lawrence and the treasure is told by Ambrose
Ambrose tells it in his book on the duties of the clergy.

games.q: you're Lawrence. a Roman official orders you to hand over the Church's treasure. what do you bring?
o: the poor, the sick and the widows.
games.why: as Ambrose tells it, Lawrence gathered the poor and said: these are the treasures of the Church.

practice: Think of someone the world tends to overlook: a janitor, an elderly neighbor, a relative who repeats themselves, someone on the street you walk past.

Picture their face as Lawrence would have seen it, a treasure, and then one small act of respect you could show them: looking them in the eye, asking how they are and waiting for the answer, listening a little longer.
If you pray, you can pray for them by name.

wordCard.voice: Human dignity. The worth of every person, which Catholics say comes from being made in God's image, not from being useful. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: worth, the standing that deserves respect.

carryVoice: Your line: dignity is given. The treasure is still walking the streets. See you tomorrow.
